title: The time of Vespasian
hook: picture Vespasian's age: marrying, farming, flattering, all gone (Meditations 4.32)

segments.voice: Yesterday: do less, only what's necessary. Your line was ask who actually needs me now.

Find an old photograph of your street from about a hundred years ago. A man in a hat hurrying somewhere. Two women talking outside a shop. A boy with a bicycle. Each of them was in the middle of something urgent: a debt, a crush, a quarrel with a brother. Every one of those urgencies is finished now. Marcus Aurelius did this exercise without photographs, using an emperor from an earlier generation of Rome.
screen: `A PHOTO OF YOUR STREET, 100 YEARS AGO.` → `EVERYONE IN IT, IN A HURRY.` → `THE TIME OF VESPASIAN.`

segments.voice: Think of the times of Vespasian, Marcus writes in book four, entry thirty-two. Vespasian was an emperor from before Marcus's time. And what do you see? People marrying, raising children, getting sick, dying, fighting wars, feasting, trading, farming, flattering, being stubbornly proud, suspecting, plotting, wishing others dead, grumbling at the present, loving, piling up treasure, longing for high office and for power. Everything people did then, and do now. And that whole life of theirs, Marcus says, no longer exists anywhere. Then he does it again with the emperor Trajan's time, a little closer. Same list. Also gone. He isn't doing this to feel gloomy or superior. He's doing it to measure. The quarrel that feels enormous this week is the same size as the quarrels in Vespasian's Rome. Look, he says, at how many threw themselves into these things, and then fell, and came apart. What lasts, for him, is not the outcome of the hurry. It's whether, in the middle of it, a person kept to what is right. The exercise shrinks the hurry, not the good. The worries get smaller. Character doesn't.
screen: `THINK OF THE TIMES OF VESPASIAN.` · `MARRYING, FARMING, FLATTERING, PLOTTING.` · `THAT WHOLE LIFE IS GONE.` · `IT SHRINKS THE HURRY, NOT THE GOOD.` · then, large: `ALL GONE.`

segments.voice: Picture the place you live a century ago: the same ground, different buildings, people walking and worrying, each one sure their worry was the big one. Then set one worry of your own among them, and notice its size there. What's left that still matters?
Vespasian. Marcus pictures Vespasian's Rome, marrying, farming, flattering, plotting, and notes that all of it is gone. Today's word.
Your line: all gone. Every urgency in that old photograph has finished. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes picture their own town a century ago, as in Meditations 4.32, to see their present worries at their true size.

Vespasian.meaning: a Roman emperor from before Marcus's time

Trajan.meaning: a later Roman emperor whose time Marcus pictures next

Marcus Aurelius.meaning: Roman emperor and Stoic who wrote the Meditations to himself

notes: 4.32 paraphrased: consider the times of Vespasian: people marrying, bringing up children, sick, dying, warring, feasting, trafficking, cultivating the ground, flattering, obstinately arrogant, suspecting, plotting, wishing for some to die, grumbling about the present, loving, heaping up treasure, desiring consulship and kingly power; that life no longer exists; then the times of Trajan, all the same, also dead; consider how many after great efforts soon fell and were resolved into the elements. Confirm list and the 'fell and came apart' phrasing.
Vespasian reigned 69–79 CE; Trajan 98–117 CE. Confirm.
The trapdoor's observation that the exercise moves forward toward Marcus's own time is interpretive; confirm.
